accepted_concepts.label: NLP Definition
accepted_concepts.description: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a subfield of AI that focuses on enabling computers to understand, process, and derive meaning from human language, leveraging linguistics and computer science, often relying on statistical approximations.

accepted_concepts.label: NLP Challenges
accepted_concepts.description: Natural Language Processing faces fundamental difficulties including text segmentation, ambiguity, context interpretation, semantic extraction, and the inherent variability of natural language where similar words can have different meanings and identical meanings can be expressed differently, making it distinct from processing structured data.

Describe how ambiguity can make interpretation difficult with an example.

They cover overlapping facets like ambiguity and add complementary aspects (segmentation, context, vs. variability, distinctness from tabular data). They are at the same definitional level and can be taught as one cohesive concept.

accepted_concepts.label: Text Preprocessing and Normalization
accepted_concepts.description: The essential steps of cleaning and standardizing raw text for NLP, including lowercasing, removing punctuation, special characters, HTML tags, stop words, and tokenization, to reduce noise and ensure uniformity.

Apply preprocessing to a given raw text sample, including lowercasing, removing punctuation and stop words, and tokenization.

accepted_concepts.label: Bag-of-Words Model Definition and Vocabulary Construction
accepted_concepts.description: The bag-of-words (BOW) model represents documents as fixed-length vectors of word counts, using a vocabulary built from unique words across the corpus. Word order and grammar are disregarded, and documents are represented as vectors with each dimension corresponding to a vocabulary word.
coverage_criteria: Define the BOW model and explain how it converts text into word count vectors, disregarding word order and grammar.
Define vocabulary in BOW, explain how it determines vector dimensions, and how out-of-vocabulary words are handled.
accepted_concepts.merge_rationale: These candidates both define core aspects of the bag-of-words model at the definition level. The vocabulary construction is an integral part of understanding how BOW works and is typically taught together. They represent one teachable concept.

accepted_concepts.label: Bag of Words with scikit-learn's CountVectorizer
accepted_concepts.description: Using CountVectorizer from scikit-learn to convert text documents into a term-document matrix of token counts. Students configure parameters such as max_features, n-gram range, and preprocessing options, then apply fit_transform to generate the matrix and interpret the output.
coverage_criteria: Instantiate CountVectorizer with parameters like max_features and fit_transform a list of texts to obtain a sparse matrix.
Explain how parameters (e.g., max_features) control vocabulary size and interpret the resulting term-document matrix.
accepted_concepts.merge_rationale: Both candidates teach the identical concept of implementing Bag of Words using scikit-learn's CountVectorizer at the implementation level. They cover instantiation, fit_transform, and parameter tuning (including max_features). Despite minor wording differences and lesson contexts, they represent the same teachable idea and can be assessed with the same questions.

accepted_concepts.label: TF-IDF Definition and Computation
accepted_concepts.description: TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) is a statistical measure used to evaluate the importance of a term to a document in a corpus. It is computed as the product of term frequency (TF), normalized by document length, and inverse document frequency (IDF), which scales down terms that appear in many documents. The resulting weight highlights terms that are frequent in a specific document but rare across the corpus.
coverage_criteria: Define TF-IDF and its components (TF and IDF), and explain its purpose in highlighting important words.
Compute TF, IDF, and TF-IDF for a given term in a small corpus.
Explain why TF-IDF improves over simple term frequency and identify when to use it in text analysis.
accepted_concepts.merge_rationale: Both candidates teach the definition and computation of TF-IDF at the same implementation depth, covering the same core concepts and techniques. They are essentially the same subject concept, presented in different lessons.

accepted_concepts.label: TF-IDF concept and TfidfVectorizer weighting

accepted_concepts.merge_rationale: This candidate teaches the theoretical underpinning of TF-IDF, which is a standalone subject concept.

accepted_concepts.label: Implementing TF-IDF with TfidfVectorizer in Python

accepted_concepts.merge_rationale: This candidate teaches the practical implementation of TF-IDF in code, which is a distinct hands-on skill from the conceptual explanation.

accepted_concepts.label: One-Hot Encoding Definition

accepted_concepts.label: Distributional Hypothesis
accepted_concepts.description: The distributional hypothesis states that words occurring in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. It is the foundation for distributional semantics and word embeddings, allowing meaning to be inferred from contextual usage patterns.
coverage_criteria: State the distributional hypothesis.
Explain how the hypothesis justifies using word embeddings to represent meaning.

Although one focuses on word embeddings and the other on contextual similarity including antonyms, they teach the identical core concept without introducing a deeper mechanism or broader application. They are same-level duplicates and can be merged.

accepted_concepts.label: Word Embeddings as Dense Vector Representations
accepted_concepts.description: Words can be represented as dense, low-dimensional vectors in a continuous space, where semantically similar words have similar vectors, and vector dimensions capture latent semantic features. This contrasts with sparse representations like one-hot or bag-of-words.

They cover definition, semantic similarity, analogies, and feature dimensions, which are facets of the same core concept. They are testable with a unified set of questions about the nature of embeddings.

accepted_concepts.label: Similarity Measures for Word Vectors: Cosine and Euclidean
